passage:
The meetinghouse bell in Tessel Hollow came over the pass on an ox sled in 1841, after the town had saved for it for eleven years. Near the top the sled broke an axle, and the men carried the bell the last mile on poles. My grandfather had rung it at noon for decades, and it had a deep, round voice, but the story of its arrival was what he told me most.

The winter I turned twelve, a Mr. Fenn came from the city to tune the meetinghouse organ. He was the first to hear it: at noon on his second day he frowned at the ceiling and asked my grandfather whether he knew his bell was cracked. Reverend Coombe had thought the new rasp was ice, and my mother had blamed the wind, but Mr. Fenn climbed the tower and showed us the crack.

At the town meeting in March, the warrant listed one proposal: send the bell to the foundry at Ludd to be recast. My grandfather rose and asked who in the room had carried it up the pass. Nobody had, but several had grandfathers who did. By the end of the evening the recasting article had been struck from the warrant, and Mr. Pruett's idea of selling to a collector in Brask got even fewer votes.

What the town did instead was my grandfather's idea. In May the bell was set on a stone base in the schoolyard, beside a plaque naming the men who had hauled it. A few people grumbled that it would have been more useful as a fire alarm, and some had wanted it rung cracked as before, but he said a bell that old belonged where children would ask about it. A smaller bell went up in the tower.

It is still there. Children climb on it and knock on its side to hear the dull clunk, and every fall the third grade learns about the ox sled. When I walk past, I put my hand on the cool green metal, and think that it ended up in exactly the right place. My sister says it looks lonely out there; I have never thought so.

options.A: the decision to sell the cracked bell to a collector
options.B: the decision to store the cracked bell in a family barn
options.C: the decision to display the cracked bell at the school
options.D: the decision to keep ringing the cracked bell as it was
options.E: the decision to melt down the cracked bell and recast it

passage:
For more than two centuries, the stone well at the center of Tessendale had a habit shared by no other well in the county. On certain evenings it hummed, a low, steady note that rose from the shaft and carried as far as the churchyard. The villagers called it the Piper's Well, and few of them wanted it explained.

The village council had other worries. After every heavy storm the well's water ran brown for days, and two families had fallen ill the previous autumn. In the spring of 1891 the council wrote to the county for a surveyor who could say whether the well was safe to keep.

The surveyor, Agathe Lorne, heard the theories first. The miller, Josiah Fenn, was sure the sound was his own wheel across the valley, carried through the rock, and a visiting naturalist had heard toads in the walls. Lorne kept a log through the summer. The hum came whether the wheel turned or stood, and long after the toads had gone quiet in June; it followed the rain, swelling in the weeks after a downpour. Lowering a weighted line, she found that the shaft opened at its base onto a hollow where an underground stream fell several feet. The falling water was the piper, and the same stream carried mud from the hillside into the well.

Some villagers asked for a pump to lift water from higher in the shaft, and the vicar wanted a stone slab laid over it so the hum could still be heard. The council judged the stream too close to mend. In October it drew twelve pounds from the parish fund for cartloads of earth, and once the ground had settled, turf was laid.

It is tempting to mourn the piper, but the legend has much to answer for. For decades it made the village treat a failing well as something sacred, and families went on drinking brown water out of respect for a drowned boy who, by every record Lorne could find, had never existed. Children now play ball on the square of grass by the church where he was said to play his pipe.

options.A: how the hum was traced to toads living in the well's walls
options.B: how the hum was traced to a stream running beneath the well
options.C: how the hum was traced to a mill wheel across the valley
options.D: how the hum was traced to wind passing over the well
